proposals.impact: lifts Money Worship open rate from 37.5% toward the 52-66% range of sister sequences
proposals.observation: The Money Worship automation has the lowest open rate of the three active sequences: 37.5% (6 opens from 16 sends). Money Vigilance sits at 66.67% and Money Avoidance at 52.63%. The gap is not volume noise at these small numbers — it is a 29-percentage-point spread against Money Vigilance. The most likely cause at this stage of a sequence is a weak subject line on email 1, because email 1 sets the open habit for the rest of the automation. A subject line that reads like a category label ("Money Worship: what it means for you") will underperform one that names the exact feeling the subscriber just admitted to in the quiz.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the subject line of email 1 in the Money Worship automation to name the specific uncomfortable truth of the money worship pattern — the person who ties their self-worth so tightly to their net worth that checking the balance becomes a form of self-assessment. The current subject line (captured below as CURRENT_TEXT) is generic enough that it could belong to any financial newsletter. The replacement should name a moment, not a concept. It must pass the Sultanic test: could 1,000 other coaches write this exact line? If yes, rewrite it.

title: "Why do I earn well but still have nothing left at the end of the month?"
pubDate: "2026-07-07"
draft: false
description: "A look at the gap between income and savings — and why closing it is less about budgeting harder and more about noticing what spending is quietly doing for you."
---

Most people assume the savings problem is a maths problem. Earn more, spend less, the gap closes. Joel earned enough to fill a gym bag with cash and still had no savings plan. The number in his account was not the problem. The question worth sitting with is what the spending was solving for — and whether you have ever actually looked at that honestly.

If the answer is no, that is not a character flaw. It is the thing worth turning toward.

---
title: "Why do I keep opening ISA comparison tabs and then closing them without doing anything?"
pubDate: "2026-07-08"
draft: false
description: "On the gap between researching money and moving money — and what that gap is usually protecting you from."
---

The tab opens. You read three paragraphs. You close it. Two weeks later, you open a different tab. Same result. This is not laziness and it is not confusion about the products. The research loop is doing something. It creates the feeling of forward motion without requiring any actual decision. A decision would make the number real. The number being real would mean you would have to reckon with it. That reckoning is the work underneath the tab-closing — not the ISA comparison itself.
